The scientific consensus from multiple controlled studies and meta-analyses is that sugar does not cause hyperactivity in children. [d3] reports that twelve double-blind, placebo-controlled studies "failed to provide any evidence that sugar ingestion leads to untoward behavior in children with Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder or in normal children." [d7] similarly cites a JAMA meta-analysis of sixteen studies concluding that "sugar doesn't affect children's behavior or cognitive performance," and [d2] echoes this, stating that "research consistently finds that eating sugar does not impact the behavior of children." [d1] and [d6] further explain that perceived hyperactivity is largely driven by parental expectation—in one study, mothers told their children had consumed sugar rated them as more hyperactive even though no sugar was given.

However, some sources present conflicting views. [d4] quotes practitioners claiming that "excessive sugar and caffeine intake both cause symptoms of hyperactivity and easy distractibility," and that candy and frosting "can lead to hyperactivity and other ADHD symptoms." [d5] cites studies suggesting high glycemic foods can cause hyperactivity and that fructose may trigger a hyperactive foraging response linked to ADHD symptoms. [d8] claims that "even children without ADHD can become fidgety and inattentive after ingesting sugar" and that sugar worsens ADHD by increasing brain dysregulation, though it also acknowledges no studies indicate sugar causes ADHD itself.

In summary, the higher-credibility peer-reviewed evidence [d1][d2][d3][d6][d7] consistently finds no causal link between sugar and hyperactivity, while some practitioner opinions and alternative theories [d4][d5][d8] suggest sugar may worsen behavior, particularly in children already diagnosed with ADHD—reflecting genuinely conflicting opinions and research outcomes on this topic.
